title: ORDER BY Without an Index Means a Sort
description: Returning the top N by an unindexed column sorts the whole table first; an index in that order reads just the first N. Why it matters: "show me the latest N" is one of the most common UI patterns there is, and an unindexed sort is a silent, ever-worsening tax on every page load.
narrative:
## What This Lesson Is About
This lesson repeats an important idea from earlier — that `ORDER BY` on an unindexed column forces an expensive sort — this time using an alphabetical example (book titles) to make the pattern land in a different, very relatable context.

Why does this happen? Rows on disk live in whatever order the table's main structure defines — here, some internal order that has nothing to do with alphabetical title order. Asking for "the first 50 books alphabetically" when nothing is stored alphabetically means SQL Server must first gather every row, sort all 200,000 titles from A to Z, and only *then** pick the first 50 off the top of that freshly sorted pile.

Imagine a bookstore where books are shelved by the order they arrived, not alphabetically. If a customer asks "show me the first 50 books alphabetically," the clerk has to pull every single book off every shelf, physically sort the entire pile A-to-Z, and only then hand over the top 50 — even though the customer only wanted 50 books. If instead the shelves were already organized alphabetically, the clerk could just walk to the "A" section and start handing over books — no sorting required. That's the value of an index that matches your `ORDER BY`: the sort is already done for you, once, up front, instead of redone every time someone runs the query.

## Scenario
A catalog page shows the first 50 books alphabetically by title. There's no index on `Title`, so returning 50 rows makes SQL Server order all 200,000 first.

## Why it's slow
`ORDER BY Title` on an unindexed column forces an explicit **Sort** operator: the engine reads every row, sorts the whole set in memory (or tempdb), and only then takes the top 50. The sort — not the reading — dominates the cost, and it grows with the table.

## What to look for
- A **Sort** operator above a full scan, feeding a Top.
- Work proportional to the whole table even though only 50 rows are returned.

## The concept
An index stores its keys **already sorted**. Create one on `Title` (INCLUDE the columns you display) and the query just reads the first 50 entries in index order — the **Sort disappears** entirely. An index that matches your `ORDER BY` is the cheapest way to serve sorted and top-N queries.
hints: There's no index on Title, so the whole table must be sorted before the top 50 can be taken.
An index keeps keys in sorted order — reading it in order removes the need for a Sort operator.
CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_Books_Title ON Books(Title) INCLUDE (Price); then re-run.
